abstract: Schizophrenia is associated with impaired sensory gating and abnormalities in neural processing. The objectives of this study were to investigate differences in EEG signals between schizophrenia cases and controls, assess the ability of EEG-derived features to predict case-control status, and determine whether discrimination between cases and controls varied across sensory conditions. To achieve these aims, spline smoothing, permutation t-tests, Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA), Multilevel Functional Principal Component Analysis (mFPCA), K-means clustering, elastic net regression, and ridge regression were applied to EEG data collected under multiple sensory conditions. The results demonstrated that differences in brain activity between cases and controls varied across sensory conditions, with some conditions exhibiting stronger group differences than others. These findings provide further evidence of impaired sensory gating in schizophrenia. K-means clustering of FPCA and mFPCA scores revealed partial separation between cases and controls, indicating that the extracted functional features captured meaningful differences in EEG activity between the two groups. Classification models based on mFPCA scores achieved strong predictive performance, with the best elastic net models achieving an AUC greater than 0.90 and classification accuracies exceeding 70%. Overall, the findings suggest that EEG-derived functional features can distinguish between schizophrenia cases and controls, particularly when information from multiple sensory conditions is combined. The results highlight the potential of combining mFPCA with penalised regression methods for the analysis of high-dimensional EEG data and support further investigation of these approaches.

# Introduction
\label{sec:intro}
An electroencephalogram (EEG) is a non-invasive test used to measure electrical activity in the brain by attaching 64 sensor nodes to the scalp. Each sensor measures a single curve, so each test produces 64 curves. The data from EEG is commonly used to diagnose conditions such as sleep disorders, seizures and schizophrenia.

Schizophrenia is a mental health condition which is associated with unusual activity in the frontal and prefrontal sections of the brain. According to Insel, T., schizophrenia presents with "paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations late in adolescence or in early adulthood" [@Insel2010].

Sensory gating is the process by which the brain filters repeated, expected or redundant stimuli. This process is impaired in individuals with schizophrenia, particularly at the P50 (indicating pre-attentive filtering of sensory information), N100 and P200 (both reflecting the attention triggering/allocation process) regions of the EEG curve, which occur 50, 100 and 200 ms after an auditory stimulus, respectively. The impairment of the sensory gating process can be detected by a difference in the amplitude of these deflections in the curve [@Shen2020; @BOUTROS2009].

Functional data analysis (FDA) is a method of statistical analysis that analyses each function as an individual sample, as opposed to considering all the points along the curve separately. It is used when the underlying curve is smooth and continuous [@RamsaySilverman2005]. EEG curves are a type of functional data that indicates the brain's electrical activity by the continuous flow of voltages over time. FDA helps to effectively describe and interpret inherit changes in EEG signals and its relationship with human behaviours, making it an interpretable approach. In particular, Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) has been widely used to represent high-dimensional functional observations. However, standard FPCA assumes that each functional observation is independent, and so, does not naturally allow for analysis of repeated measurements.

Previous studies have investigated schizophrenia using EEG data to identify abnormalities in sensory processing and sensory gating (e.g. @BOUTROS2009, @Shen2020). Many analyses have focused on specific EEG features, such as amplitudes and latencies at predefined regions of the signal, while others have applied machine learning (ML) methods to extracted EEG features. It is clear that these approaches create valuable insights, however, information is often discarded contained within the full EEG trajectory.

At present, researchers have been using FDA to study EEG data using differing techniques. Yi Yuyan et al. [@yi2022classification] explored classification of EEG signals using functional data analysis. This research involved feature extraction and dimension reduction via FDA in a study consisting of healthy adults, where the aim was to classify long versus short distance travel. Similar to our approach, multiple trials and multiple electrodes were analysed for penalised functional logistic regression. However, the hierarchical structure of repeated trials within subjects was not explicitly modelled, with trials instead treated as separate observations.

To address the hierarchical nature of complex data, Hasenstab et al. (2017) [@hasenstab2017multidimensional] used Multidimensional FPCA to preserve the structure of EEG data collected from children with autism spectrum disorder. Their study incorporated multiple trials (120 per participant) and multiple nodes, with the main analysis focuses on four nodes from right frontal region. However, the work primarily focused on understanding variation within the data, whereas the current study investigates whether FPCA-derived features can be used to discriminate between schizophrenia cases and controls through predictive modelling and clustering.

The main foundation for this current study was introduced by Di et al. (2009) [@Di2009] who developed Multilevel Functional Principal Component Analysis (mFPCA) using sleep EEG data collected at two visits per subject. While this study established the mFPCA framework for analysing hierarchical functional data, its focus was on methodological development rather than the clustering and classification of mFPCA-derived scores.

Together, these studies display the value of using FDA and multilevel approaches for the analysis of complex EEG data. However, limited research has applied mFPCA specifically to schizophrenia EEG data while also evaluating these PC scores within predictive modelling frameworks. This study aims to address this gap.

In EEG experiments, subjects typically complete multiple trials under the same experimental condition to obtain a more reliable estimate of the neural response. Multilevel Functional Principal Component Analysis (mFPCA) extends FPCA by separating variation into between-subject and within-trial variation. This framework, therefore, provides a more appropriate representation of repeated-measures EEG data and motivates the methodology adopted in the present study.

	
## Aims

The aims of our analysis were as follows:
 
1. To investigate whether EEG signals differ between schizophrenia cases and controls during the sensory conditions detailed above
2. To develop a prediction model using FDA to accurately predict case control status
3. To investigate how condition 1 differs from condition 2 and 3 in cases and controls, as we would expect more sensory gating in condition 1 compared to the other two conditions since the sound was expected due to subjects pressing the button. Therefore, we expect that the largest difference between cases and controls EEG signals will occur in condition 1, as cases are expected to exhibit impaired sensory gating.

## Data

Our data were taken from the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH project number R01MH058262), available from [Kaggle](www.kaggle.com/datasets/broach/button-tone-sz/data)

In our data, 40 subjects underwent three sensory conditions (25 controls, 15 cases) in which:

1.  Subjects press a button to immediately produce a sound
2.  Subjects passively listen to the same sound without pressing a button
3.  Subjects press a button, and no sound is produced.


Each subject completed each of these sensory conditions up to 100 times. Therefore, we have many repetitions of the same conditions for each of the subjects. So in total we have approximately $64\times 40 \times 100 = 256,000$ curves. Data from case participants were compared with age- and gender-matched controls. Only right-handed subjects were included in this analysis [@ford2014did].

EEG recordings were obtained from 64 scalp electrodes and signals were continuously digitised at 1024 Hz, meaning that electrical activity was recorded 1024 times per second [@ford2014did]. The location of the electrodes used throughout this study is shown in Figure below.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 20, fig.asp = 1, fig.cap = "EEG Cap Sensor Labels", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics("Images/EEG_cap.png")

```
Previous studies investigating electrophysiological abnormalities in schizophrenia have reported altered neural activity in the prefrontal and frontal regions of the brain. Therefore, the primary analysis focused on the FP1 (prefrontal) and F3 (frontal) electrodes, with a secondary analysis examining the F7 and AF7 electrodes [@SenkowskiGallinat2015; @JeonPolich2003; @Shin2011].

Before any modelling was performed, the data were divided into training and test sets to obtain an unbiased assessment of model performance and to evaluate the generalisability of the resulting models. The dataset was split into 70% training data and 30% test data. To account for the repeated observations within individuals, the data were grouped by participant ID such that all observations from a given individual were assigned to the same dataset. In addition, stratified sampling was performed by group to ensure that both cases and controls were represented in the training and test sets.


# Methods

\label{sec:methods}

This section describes the statistical and machine learning methods used to analyse the EEG data and transform the raw signals into interpretable results. Spline smoothing was first applied to reduce noise while preserving the underlying structure of the EEG signals. Permutation t-tests were used to assess differences between the mean functional curves of cases and controls. Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) and Multilevel Functional Principal Component Analysis (mFPCA) were employed to characterise the major sources of variation in the data and reduce dimensionality. K-means clustering was used to explore similarities and differences between cases and controls. Finally, elastic net regularisation was applied for variable selection and predictive modelling. Methods used to evaluate model performance, including discrimination, calibration, and classification accuracy, are also described.

## Smoothing

Due to the inherently noisy nature of EEG signals, smoothing was applied to the functional observations. When smoothing functions, it is important to balance the trade-off between variance and bias. Variance refers to the sensitivity of an estimated function to random fluctuations in the observed data, while bias refers to systematic deviation of the estimated function from the true underlying signal. High variance may lead to over-fitting and poor generalisability to new data, whereas high bias may over-smooth the data leading to under-fitting and obscuring important signal characteristics.

Spline smoothing uses piece-wise polynomial functions joined smoothly through points called knots to estimate the underlying smoothed curve and reduce noise in the data. Spline smoothing was used to reduce noise while preserving the underlying brain activity patterns. Specifically, 100 cubic B-spline basis functions were defined over the domain of each EEG signal, (0-1638ms). Using a relatively large number of basis functions provides sufficient flexibility to represent complex functional features while allowing smoothness to be controlled separately through penalisation.

A second-derivative roughness penalty was then applied. In penalised smoothing approaches, smoothness is controlled by incorporating a roughness penalty into the objective function used to fit the data, rather than by restricting the number of basis functions available [@RamsaySilverman2005]. Penalising the second derivative discourages rapid changes in curvature, allowing gradual variation in the fitted function while reducing excessive wiggliness. In practice, this encourages neighbouring B-spline coefficients to vary smoothly and can be viewed as approximating penalties on finite differences between adjacent coefficients. The roughness penalty pools information across neighbouring regions of the function, resulting in more stable estimates and reduced sensitivity to noise. Consequently, variance is reduced at the cost of a small increase in bias, yielding smoother and more interpretable functional representations of the EEG signals [@RamsaySilverman2005; @Gertheiss2024]. This can be seen in the two plots below, which compare the raw EEG curves with the corresponding smoothed curves. The raw curves exhibit substantial noise and high variability, whereas the smoothed curves provide a clearer representation of the underlying signal by reducing random variation.

Given a set of observations $\{t_i, y_i: i=1,2,...,n\}$, spline smoothing estimates a curve $X(t_i)$ from our observations assuming $y_i = X(t_i) + \epsilon_i$ where $t_i$ represents the time points along the x-axis of the curve, $X(t_i)$ represents the true underlying curve and $\epsilon_i ~ iid(0, \sigma^2)$ represents the exogenous error, which contributes to the roughness of the raw data.

We estimate $X(t)$ by minimising the following:

$$\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - X(t_i))^2 + \lambda \int [X''(t)]^2 dt$$

Where $\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - X(t_i))^2$ is the residual sum of square (RSS) and $\int [X''(t)]^2 dt$ is a penalty that prevents excessive wiggliness by preventing it from changing slope too quickly (as $X''(t)$ measures the rate of change of the slope) and $\lambda$ is the smoothing parameter where $\lambda = 0$ is the $RSS$ fit which is excessively wiggly and $\lambda \rightarrow \infty$ is over-smoothed and under-fit.

We estimate $X(t)$ by assuming that $X(t) = \sum_{k=1}^K c_k B_k(t)$ where $B_k(t)$ are the cubic basis functions that we know, $K =100$ is the total number of knots that have been selected which are equally spaced along the x-axis and $c_k$ are the coefficients of the cubic b-splines we are estimating.
```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="89%", out.height="7cm", fig.cap = "Plots of raw and smoothed data, coloured by case-control status", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics("Images/raw_vs_smoothed.png")

```

## Permutation t-test

Permutation t-tests were used to assess differences in functional EEG trajectories between cases and controls. Permutation-based inference is well suited to functional data and has been widely applied in the FDA literature [@BugniHorowitz2021]. The test evaluates the null hypothesis that the mean functions of the two groups are equal across the domain of the EEG signal.

Under the null hypothesis, group labels are exchangeable, meaning that randomly reallocating observations between groups should not systematically alter the value of the test statistic. The permutation procedure repeatedly shuffles the case-control labels and recalculates the test statistic for each permutation, generating an empirical null distribution. The observed test statistic is then compared with this distribution to determine statistical significance. The resulting p-value represents the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as that observed if the null hypothesis were true.

When interpreting a permutation t-test plot for an a priori, theory-driven hypothesis, statistical significance is indicated when the observed test statistic exceeds the pointwise $0.05$ critical value. However, for post hoc, data-driven hypotheses, significance should be assessed relative to the maximum $0.05$ critical value, which controls for multiple comparisons across the entire functional domain and provides stronger control of the family-wise error rate, (Bugni and Horowitz, 2021).

In this study, five thousand permutation t-tests were applied to the FP1 electrode on a condition-by-condition basis. The FP1 region was selected due to previous evidence linking frontal EEG abnormalities, particularly gamma-band dysfunction, to schizophrenia and associated cognitive deficits [@SenkowskiGallinat2015; @JeonPolich2003; @Shin2011].

## Functional Principal Component Analysis

Following smoothing, each EEG recording was represented as a continuous function observed over 1,638 time points. Although, as mentioned above, smoothing reduces noise and improves interpretability, functional observations remain high-dimensional. As discussed by J.O Ramsay et al. [@RamsaySilverman2005], this data may display a small number of dominant modes of variation - to identify and explore these, principal component analysis was applied to functional data.

In functional PCA, eigenvalues of the bivariate variance-covariance function $\nu(s,t)$ denote the importance of each principal component. An eigenfunction is associated with each eigenvalue, and these describe major variational components.

Due to the inherently high-dimensional nature of EEG data, directly analysing observations can be challenging. FPCA addresses this issue by representing each function as a linear combination of a small number of eigenfunctions, this allows the dominant sources of variation to be captured through a reduced set of principal component scores.

### FPCA via PACE

Functional Principal Component Analysis was implemented using the Principal Analysis by Conditional Estimation (PACE) method, developed by @yao2005PACE. This package is useful for the analysis of data that have been generated alongside noise, irregular time points or sparse data. A key advantage of the PACE method is that it can be used for sparsely or densely sampled random trajectories - the EEG recordings analysed in this study can be considered as densely sampled data, as each EEG curve was observed across a large number of time points on the same time grid. Here, PACE was used to estimate the principal modes of variation in the EEG curves and obtain subject-specific FPCA scores (FPCs).

Each participant contributed a single densely sampled EEG curve corresponding to Trial 1 at the FP1 electrode under Condition 1.

### FPCA Formula

Each EEG curve is decomposed into: (1) a mean function; (2) eigenfunctions describing major modes of variation, and; (3) subject-specific FPCA scores.

The curves are decomposed by the Karhunen-Loève expansion as follows:

$$X_i (t) = \mu (t) + \sum_{k=1}^K \xi_{ik} \Phi_k (t)$$ where $\mu(t)$ is the mean function, $\xi_{ik} = \int_0^1 (X_i(t) - \mu(t))\Phi_k(t)  dt$ are the FPC scores.

Using the PACE method, however we estimate the FPC scores as follows:

Given the smoothed random functions $X_i(t)$ we first estimate the mean function $\hat\mu(t)$ for all these observations (curves) from all subjects in the training data. Then, we estimate the covariance function $Cov(X (s), X (t)) = G(s, t)$. If we perform eigendecomposition of this covariance function to get eigenvalues $e_k$ and eigenfunctions $\Phi_k(t)$ which are the FPCs we were looking for. The corresponding FPC scores $\xi_{ik}$ can be estimated from these the observations, the mean function and the eigenvalues and functions [@yao2005PACE]. Components explaining up to 95% of the total variability were retained for subsequent analyses.


### Exploring FPCA scores via extreme curve and then k-means clustering

K-means clustering was subsequently applied to the scores to determine if there was any pattern in the data. K-means clustering is an unsupervised learning algorithm which groups unlabelled data into K-distinct clusters by choosing a random point as a center (centroid) for the cluster and assigning each observation to the nearest cluster (using Euclidean distance). Then finding the mean point for all points in the cluster, it uses this as a new centroid and continues iterates the process until the centroids become stable.

As quoted from Fortuna F. "cluster analysis aims to group a set of data such that units within clusters are more similar than across clusters with respect to a metric. In the FDA context, the most popular technique is the k-means clustering algorithm" [@FortunaMaturo2019].

To establish an appropriate number of clusters for our k-means analysis, several values of $k$ were explored and a four-cluster solution was selected. This number was chosen as it provided a reasonable balance between cluster separation and interpretability. Given the relatively small sample size, large numbers of clusters would have resulted in very small cluster memberships. The aim of this is to investigate whether subjects with similar FPCA score patterns group together naturally. The resulting clusters were compared with schizophrenia status using a confusion matrix, and smoothed EEG curves were then plotted within each cluster. This analysis was used to assess whether FPCA scores captured patterns in the EEG data that could be relevant for differentiating between schizophrenia cases and controls.

## Logistic Regression Model

According to Lan N. Bui, "Logistic regression is commonly utilized in clinical and educational research to examine relationships between risk factors and binary outcomes" [@BuiDing2025]. Following FPCA, logistic regression models were fitted to examine whether FPCA scores were associated with the classification of schizophrenia (group = 1). 

The multiple logistic regression model is given by:
$$ \log(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \cdots + \beta_pX_p$$

Where $Y$ denotes the binary response $= (0,1)$, $(\pi)$ represents the proportion (probability) of $1$'s at any combination of predictor values $(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p)$, and $(\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_p)$ are the corresponding regression coefficients.  

Equivalently, the probability $(\pi)$ can be expressed as:

$$ \frac{\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \cdots + \beta_pX_p)}{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \cdots + \beta_pX_p)} $$

In this study, schizophrenia status was treated as the binary outcome variable and the first three FPCA scores were used as predictors. The purpose of this analysis was to assess whether the selected three FPCA scores contained significant information to discriminate between schizophrenia cases and controls. Odds ratios were also calculated to aid interpretation of the resulting fitted coefficients. 


## Multilevel Functional Principal Component Analysis

At this stage in analysis, the EEG curves of subjects within one trial and one condition were investigated. To extend this, and include several of the repeated trials per subject and conditions, one could no longer use standard FPCA.

An important limitation of standard FPCA methods is that they are not designed for multilevel analyses, due to their assumption of independence between observations. Introduced in @Di2009, multilevel FPCA was designed to address the volume and importance of EEG data specifically. This methodology is designed to extract core intra- and inter- subject components of multilevel functional data.

### Arranging multilevel functional data

To accurately arrange the repeated structure, all available trials were retained and smoothed using the same B-spline smoothing procedure described previously for standard FPCA. The data were then reorganised into a long-format data structure, where each observation consisted of a subject ID, trial number, time point and the corresponding smoothed EEG value. By organising the data into this format, repeated functional observations from the same individual can be linked together during later analysis.

mFPCA was implemented using the `mFPCA.face()` function [@LiCui2024]. The smoothed EEG curves were arranged in a matrix where each row represented a single EEG trial, each column corresponded to a time point. To separate the subject-level and trial-level variation, subject ID and trial number were included. Components were retained until $95%$ of the total variation had been explained.

The full model of mFPCA was formulated as

$$Y_{ij} = \mu(t) + \eta_j(t) + \sum^{K_1}_{k=1} \xi_{ik}\phi_k^{(1)}(t) + \sum^{K_2}_{l=1} \zeta_{ijl}\phi_l^{(2)} + \epsilon_{ij}(t)$$

[@Zablocki2024], where $Y_{ij}(t)$ is the smoothed EEG signal measured at time $(t)$ for trial $(j)$ belonging to subject $(i)$, where $(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n)$ and $(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n)$. The function $(\mu(t))$ represents the overall mean EEG trajectory across all subjects and trials, and $(\eta_j(t))$ represents the trial-specific shift from this overall mean. The term $(\epsilon_{ij}(t))$ denotes a residual error.

The functions $(\phi_k^{(1)(t))})$ and $(\phi_l^{(2)}(t))$ are the eigenfunctions at level 1 and level 2 respectively. Level 1 eigenfunctions describe between-subject variation, capturing the systematic differences in EEG signals across subjects, whereas level 2 eigenfunctions describe the within-subject variation, capturing trial-to-trial fluctuations within the same subject. The corresponding scores, $(\xi_{ik})$ and $(\zeta_{ijl})$, quantifies this variation from at a subject and trial level, described  by each eigenfunction. 

Intuitively here, each eigenfunction can be interpreted as representing a particular characteristic pattern of EEG activity. The corresponding principal component score, similar to standard FPCA, indicates the extent to which that pattern is present within an individual's EEG trajectory. Larger positive or negative scores indicate a greater differentiation from the overall mean function. Therefore, the eigenvalues associated with each component tell one the amount of variability explained by that specific component.

In order to explain 95% of the total variability in the EEG data, as set within `mfpca.face()`, an appropriate number of principal components were to be selected at both level 1 and level 2. The quantities $(K_1)$ and $(K_2)$ denote this number of retained components at level 1 and level 2 respectively. The resulting level 1 and level 2 scores represented these repeated EEG measurements in a concise way and were subsequently used in clustering and classification analyses. 

## K-Means Clustering Level 1 Scores

Following the formation of level 1 mFPCA scores, it was of interest to explore how k-means clustering of these between-patient scores compare to standard FPCA clustering results. The optimal number of clusters was explored using the elbow method based on the total within-cluster sum of squares. K-means clustering was then performed using the selected number of clusters and cluster membership was compared with schizophrenia status. 

## Elastic Net

Elastic net is a regularization and variable selection method that combines the penalties used in ridge and lasso regression. The method is controlled by a mixing parameter, $\alpha$, where $\alpha = 0$ corresponds to ridge regression and $\alpha = 1$ corresponds to lasso regression. Values of $\alpha$ between 0 and 1 provide a balance between the two approaches, [@ZouHastie2005].

In ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, coefficients are estimated by minimizing the residual sum of squares (RSS), which represents the sum of the squared differences between the observed and predicted values. Consequently, the fitted regression line is chosen to produce predictions that are as close as possible to the observed data. Ridge regression, introduced by @HoerlKennard1970, extends OLS by adding an (L_2) penalty to the objective function. This penalty constrains the magnitude of the regression coefficients by minimizing:

$$\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2$$

where $\lambda$ is a non-negative tuning parameter controlling the degree of shrinkage. By shrinking coefficients towards zero, ridge regression reduces model variance and can improve predictive performance in the presence of multicollinearity. However, coefficients are not reduced exactly to zero, meaning all predictors remain in the model. Lasso regression applies an (L_1) penalty to the regression coefficients and minimizes:

$$\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|$$

This penalty shrinks coefficients towards zero and can set some coefficients exactly equal to zero. Consequently, lasso performs automatic variable selection, removing less informative predictors and producing a more parsimonious model, [@Tibshirani1996]. Elastic net combines the (L_1) and (L_2) penalties and minimizes:

$$\mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \left[(1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2 + \alpha\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\right]$$

This approach balances the sparsity-inducing properties of lasso with the ability of ridge regression to handle correlated predictors. The mixing parameter $\alpha$ was tuned over a grid of values between 0 and 1. For each value of $\alpha$, an elastic net model was fitted and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. The value of $\alpha$ that produced the lowest cross-validated error was selected, together with its corresponding optimal penalty parameter, $\lambda$. Elastic net is particularly useful when the number of predictors exceeds the number of observations and when predictors are highly correlated. In such settings, it often provides more stable and accurate predictions than lasso regression alone [@ZouHastie2005].

# Performance Evaluation

Model performance was evaluated using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), accuracy, misclassification error rate, and calibration. 

The ROC curve assesses the ability of a classification model to distinguish between two classes, [@Fawcett2006], cases and controls in this application. ROC curves were generated in R using the pROC package, [@Robin2011]. Predicted probabilities from the classification models were evaluated across all possible classification thresholds. At each threshold, sensitivity and specificity were calculated from the resulting confusion matrix, and the ROC curve was constructed by plotting the true positive rate (sensitivity) against the false positive rate (1-specificity). These thresholds determine the predicted probability above which an observation is classified as a case (1) rather than a control (0).

The discriminatory ability of the model was quantified using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), [@Fawcett2006]. The AUC can be interpreted as the probability that a randomly selected case receives a higher predicted probability than a randomly selected control. An AUC of 0.5 indicates no discriminatory ability, whereas an AUC of 1 indicates perfect discrimination. 

Classification performance was further evaluated using a confusion matrix at a threshold of 0.5. Predicted probabilities greater than or equal to 0.5 were classified as cases, while probabilities below 0.5 were classified as controls. Accuracy was calculated as the proportion of correctly classified observations, and the misclassification error rate as the proportion incorrectly classified. The Brier score was also calculated to assess the overall accuracy of the predicted probabilities. It is defined as the mean squared difference between the observed outcomes and the predicted probabilities, with lower values indicating better predictive performance.

Calibration was assessed using calibration plots generated from the model's predicted probabilities. These plots compare predicted probabilities with observed outcome frequencies across the range of predicted risks [@Collins2014]. A well-calibrated model produces predicted probabilities that closely reflect the observed outcomes. Perfect calibration is represented by a curve lying on the diagonal reference line, corresponding to a calibration slope of 1 and an intercept of 0.


# Results

\label{sec:results}

This section presents the results obtained from the statistical and machine learning methods described in the previous methods section. Findings from the permutation t-tests, FPCA, K-means clustering, mFPCA, and elastic net analyses are reported.

## Permutation t-test

The a priori null hypothesis was that, following stimulus presentation at approximately 100 ms, there would be no difference in the mean EEG functions between cases and controls. Stimulus onset is indicated by the vertical blue reference line in the plots below. As this hypothesis was pre-specified, statistical significance was assessed relative to the pointwise 0.05 critical value. Evidence against the null hypothesis is indicated when the observed test statistic exceeds this threshold.

In Condition 1, during which participants pressed a button to immediately produce a sound, the observed test statistic exceeded the pointwise 0.05 critical value over a substantial portion of the post-stimulus interval. This provides strong evidence of differences in the EEG responses of cases and controls.

In Condition 2, during which participants passively listened to the same sound without pressing a button, the observed test statistic exceeded the pointwise 0.05 critical value over a small portion of the post-stimulus interval, suggesting evidence of differences between the groups.

In Condition 3, during which participants pressed a button, but no sound was produced, the observed test statistic did not exceed the pointwise 0.05 critical value. Consequently, there was no evidence of a difference between the EEG responses of cases and controls.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap="Permutation T-tests: (a) Condition 1; (b) Condition 2; (c) Condition 3.", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics(c(
"Images/permt_cond1.png",
"Images/permt_cond2.png",
"Images/permt_cond3.png"))

```

## Functional Principal Component Analysis

FPCA decomposes each individual curve into the mean curve plus the sum of the other principal components multiplied by a scalar (score) which indicates how much that individual curve aligns with the specific principal component.

We conducted this FPCA for a single condition and a single trial (trial 1 condition 1) since FPCA can only work on data where each person has only one curve. We chose to investigate the FPCs of condition 1 rather than the other two conditions as it showed the most significant difference in EEG signals between cases and controls according to the permutation t-test above.

```{r, echo = FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.cap = "FPCA visualisation - condition 1, trial 1", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics("Images/FPCA.png")

```

As you can see the functional principal components are eigenfunctions which explain the main modes of variation. We found we only needed three functional principal components to explain 95% of the variability in the curves.

On the top right of this plot is the mean curve, and on the bottom right, we can see the main modes of variation about this mean curve. So, the mean curve is flattened to be a straight line, and the eigenfunctions represent the functional principal components.

The first functional principal component, shown in black, remains close to the mean function initially, and then it drops below the mean. In the second FPC shown in red the eigenfunction rises above the mean and then dropping below. The third initially rises above the mean then goes below before rising above the mean again.

These are the three main ways in which subject's curves vary about the mean and as we can see from the scree plot on the bottom left we can see that the first FPC explains the most variance at approximately \~90% and the second and third describe the remaining \~5% of the variation.

### Investigating FPC scores

To observe the principal component scores look like on our actual data, we have plotted the subjects with the top and bottom scores for each FPC.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap="Curves with highest 5 FPC scores (blue) and lowest 5 scores (red): (a) FPC 1, (b) FPC 2, (c) FPC 3", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics(c("Images/FPC1_top_bot.png",
                          "Images/FPC2_top_bot.png",
                          "Images/FPC3_top_bot.png"))

```

Those with the highest scores (in blue) for the first principal component (top left figure) remain close to the mean at the beginning and go down over time, and those with the lowest scores (in red) for the first principal component remain close to the mean and then rise up above the mean over time. The top scorers following a similar trajectory to that of the first eigenfunction shown above and the lowest scorers following an inverse trajectory.

For those with the highest scores for the second functional principal component (see top right figure) they go up initially before going down. Inversely those with the lowest scores go have a downward trajectory initially before going up. Top scorers approximately follows the trajectory of the second eigenfunction and low scorers the opposite, although the similarity is not as strong as in the first principal component.

Those with the highest scores for the third principal component (plot on the bottom) they go up, then down, then up again as in the third eigenfunction. The lowest scorers as before do the opposite however, these patterns are not as distinct as the actual eigenfunction itself.

## Multi-Level Functional Principal Component Analysis

Unlike the previous FPCA analysis, which considered a single trial under a single condition, mFPCA allowed repeated EEG trials from each subject to be analysed simultaneously. This allowed variation to be broken down into Level 1 (between-subject variation) and level 2 (within-subject variation).

The first four eigenfunctions for level 1 and level 2 are shown below. Similar to FPCA, these eigenfunctions represent the dominant modes of variation within the EEG signals, explaining 95% of the variation in the curves. However, level 1 components describe differences between subjects, whereas level 2 components describe variation between repeated trials from the same subject. Comparing the FPCA eigenfunctions with the level 1 mFPCA eigenfunctions reveals notable differences in the dominant modes of variation. This is expected, as mFPCA incorporates repeated trials and separates between-subject and within-subject variation, whereas standard FPCA is based on a single functional observation per participant.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap="(a) The first four Level 1 mFPCA principal components representing between-subject variation", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics("Images/level1mfpca.png")

```

 
For level 1, above, the first principal component explains the largest proportion of between-subject variability. The first mFPC (blue) captures a broad pattern across the EEG trajectory, while the remaining components display more oscillatory behaviour. Notably, the third (red) and fourth (purple) components show substantial variation particularly surrounding $100 \ ms$, the point of stimulus onset. This suggests that differences in EEG responses during the post-stimulus period contribute meaningfully to the variability observed between subjects Together, these components summarise the primary ways in which subjects' EEG trajectories differ from one another.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap= "(b) First four Level 2 mFPCA principal components representing trial-to-trial variation" , fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics(           "Images/level2mfpca.png")
```

The level 2 mFPCs, figure (b) above, represent the dominant souces of within-subject variation across the repeated trials. Compared with the level 1 components, these appear smoother and exhibit more gradual changes over time. The first principal component (blue) displays the dominant source of between-trial variation within subjects and displays a broad decreasing trend throughout the EEG trajectory. As expected, less localised variation is observed than between-subject variation.
Unlike the level 1 components, which show substantial variation surrounding the stimulus onset period, the level 2 components do not exhibit any clear change around the $100 \ ms$ region which reflects more general fluctuations in EEG activity across repeated trials. 
However, the magnitude of the deviations from the mean function suggests that a lot of variability exists between repeated trials despite accounting for subject-level effects. This observation is expected within our analysis, as variability between different subjects is anticipated to be greater than variability observed across repeated trials from the same subject. 

Overall, the mFPCA results indicate that meaningful variation does exist at both the subject and trial levels. This information is used further as predictors in the elastic net classification model.

To determine whether the subject-level variation identified by mFPCA improved the distinction between cases and controls, k-means clustering was applied to mFPCA level 1 scores and compared with standard FPCA score clustering results. This was done as the level 1 scores and the standard FPCA scores are both working on the between-subject level.

To compare this with the kmeans clustering performed previously on the single trial data we used four clusters as before.

```

## Elastic Net

The first analysis incorporated data from four EEG nodes (fp1, f3, f7 and af7) together with mFPCA scores explaining 95% of the variability at both levels 1 and 2. Models were fitted using data from all conditions simultaneously, as well as separately for each of the three experimental conditions.


The second analysis incorporated data from two EEG nodes (fp1 and f3) together with mFPCA scores explaining 95% of the variability at both levels 1 and 2.

The third analysis incorporated data from four EEG nodes (fp1, f3, f7 and af7) together with mFPCA scores explaining 90% of the variability at both levels 1 and 2.

The fourth analysis examined the effect of ridge regression by setting $\alpha = 0$, thereby retaining all the predictors in the model as ridge regression shrinks coefficients towards zero but does not set them exactly equal to zero, and therefore does not perform variable selection. Data from four EEG nodes (fp1, f3, f7 and af7) were incorporated together with mFPCA scores explaining 95% of the variability at both levels 1 and 2.

As in the first analysis, models in the second, third and fourth analyses were fitted using data from all conditions simultaneously, as well as separately for each of the three experimental conditions. However, only the results for all conditions combined and for Condition 1 are presented in detail. The focus on Condition 1 was motivated by the permutation t-test results, which provided the strongest evidence of differences between cases and controls. Results for Conditions 2 and 3 are not presented, as these conditions showed limited evidence of group differences.

### Section 1 – four EEG nodes, with 95% variability explained

Firstly, the model was fitted on all conditions simultaneously. Using 10-fold cross-validation, the optimal tuning parameters were identified as $\alpha = 0.71$ and $\lambda = 0.000081$. The original set of 290 predictor variables was reduced to 35 non-zero coefficients (Figure a), indicating substantial variable selection. Among the mFPCA score predictors, 32 level 1 predictors were retained, while no level 2 predictors remained in the model. Model discrimination was outstanding, with an AUC of 0.937 (Figure b). The ROC curve demonstrated strong separation between cases and controls across a range of classification thresholds. Classification accuracy at a threshold of 0.5 was 74.2%. Examination of the calibration plot (Figure c) indicated imperfect calibration, with a calibration slope between 0.47 and 0.70. This was further reflected in the distribution of predicted probabilities (Figure d), where predictions tended to cluster near 0 and 1 rather than being spread across the full probability range.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap="Model performance results for all conditions, 4 nodes, 95% variability explained: (a) Coefficient Plot; (b) ROC Curve; (c) Calibration Plot; (d) Predicted Probability Plot.", fig.pos="H"}

knitr::include_graphics(c(
"Images/coefficients_allcond_4nodes_95var.png",
"Images/roc_allcond_4nodes_95var.png",
"Images/calibration_allcond_4nodes_95var.png",
"Images/predprob_allcond_4nodes_95var.png"))

```

Next the model was fitted on the conditions independently. Condition 1 obtained the optimal tuning parameters as $\alpha = 0.91$ and $\lambda = 0.000026$. The original set of 62 predictor variables was reduced to 26 non-zero coefficients (Figure a). Among the mFPCA score predictors, 21 level 1 and 4 level 2 predictors were retained. Model discrimination was acceptable, with an AUC of 0.711 (Figure b). Classification accuracy at a threshold of 0.5 was 66%. The calibration plot indicated imperfect calibration (Figure c) with a calibration slope ranging from 0.04 to 0.09. This was further reflected in the distribution of predicted probabilities (Figure d), where predictions tended to cluster near 0 and 1, indicating overly extreme predicted probabilities.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', out.width="49%", fig.width = 18, fig.asp = 0.9, fig.cap="Model performance results for condition 1, 4 nodes, 95% variability explained: (a) Coefficient Plot; (b) ROC Curve; (c) Calibration Plot; (d) Predicted Probability Plot.", fig.pos="H"}

```

### Section 4: Ridge Regression, four EEG nodes, with 95% variability explained

Alpha was set to zero, thereby fitting a ridge regression model. Firstly, the model was fitted using data from all conditions simultaneously. Using 10-fold cross-validation, the optimal shrinkage parameter was identified as $\lambda = 0.02058$. All 260 original predictors were retained in the model. Among the mFPCA score predictors, 74 Level 1 and 182 Level 2 predictors were retained. Model discrimination was good, with an AUC of 0.803 (Figure b). The ROC curve demonstrated separation between cases and controls across a range of classification thresholds. Classification accuracy at a threshold of 0.5 was 76.01%. The Brier score was 0.1634, indicating good overall predictive accuracy. Examination of the calibration plot indicated good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, with the 95% confidence interval for the calibration slope containing 1 (95% CI: 0.85 to 1.29; Figure c). However, the calibration intercept was greater than 0 (95% CI: 0.28 to 0.71), suggesting that the model tended to underestimate the probability of schizophrenia.

# Discussion

\label{sec:discussion}

This section discusses the key findings of the study and considers their implications. The results as outlined in the results section above are interpreted with particular emphasis on sensory gating, group differences between cases and controls, and the performance of the predictive modelling approaches. The strengths and limitations of the study are also considered, together with recommendations for future research.

## Permutation ttests

Sensory gating refers to the ability of the brain to filter repeated, expected, or redundant sensory stimuli and has been shown to be impaired in individuals with schizophrenia (Boutros et al., 2009; Shen et al., 2020). In the present study, the repeated stimulus was represented by an auditory tone. The observed differences between cases and controls in Conditions 1 and 2 are consistent with impaired sensory gating in schizophrenia.

The difference was most pronounced in Condition 1, where participants generated the sound themselves by pressing a button. In healthy controls, self-generated sensory events are typically attenuated because the sensory consequences of an action are anticipated. Consequently, the larger difference observed in this condition may reflect reduced suppression of predictable sensory input in individuals with schizophrenia.

In contrast, no evidence of group differences was observed in Condition 3, where participants pressed a button, but no sound was produced. The absence of a difference when no auditory stimulus was present provides further support for the interpretation that the findings are related to altered processing of expected auditory information rather than the differences in motor activity associated with pressing the button.

Overall, it is observed that permutation test results support previous evidence that sensory gating mechanisms are disrupted in schizophrenia, particularly when participants self-generate the auditory stimulus. These findings are consistent with previous research, proposing that schizophrenia is linked to impaired predictive processing.

## FPCA

FPCA was able to explain 95% of the variability in the curves by using three principal components (i.e. the three main modes of variation). Subjects with higher scores for FPC 1 had a similar trajectory to that of the eigenfunction as the score indicates how closely a curve aligns with the eigenfunction in question. The trajectories of the top scores for FPC 2 and FPC 3 followed similar trajectories to their eigenfunctions however it a was far less pronounced than similarity than that of FPC 1. This is likely due to the fact that FPC 1 explains far more of the variability in curves than FPC 2 or FPC 3.

### K-means Clustering

The k-means clusters indicate that there may be some predictive power in the FPC scores since cluster 1, 3, and 4 have membership mainly of cases or controls. Though there is some overlap in cluster 2 the other clusters tend to separate cases and controls quite well, indicating that a model using the FPC scores may have some predictive power on the case-control status.

## mFPCA

The mFPCA results demonstrated that meaningful variation existed at both subject and trial level ($1$ and $2$). The presence of substantial level 2 variability motivates the use of mFPCA, confirming that using repeated EEG trials contain valuable information rather than simply measuring noise.

Interestingly, we see differences between the mFPCA level 1 eigenfunctions and those obtained using standard FPCA. This is expected due to the additional inherently noisy EEG data across multiple conditions and repeated trials. We observe a cleaner representation of subject-level differences following the introduction of additional data, and the account for within-subject variability. This finding is consistent with previous work which suggested that between EEG trials may itself be informative in schizophrenia.


### K-means clustering

When K-means clustering was applied to the level 1 mFPCA scores, a difference was anticipated based on the fact that multiple trials were being included as as opposed to a single trial, therefore there was more information for each subject even looking at the level 1 scores. However, the overall clustering structure remained broadly similar.

Membership to cluster 1, 3 and 4 were mainly controls, while cluster 2 membership was more evenly split. This may indicate that we may be better able to predict controls than cases and that including the level 2 scores in our predictive model may improve its predictive power.

## Classification Performance (Elastic net)

This section first examines the elastic net models incorporating data from four EEG nodes, considering both the combined all-conditions model and the three individual condition-specific models. The performance of these four-node models is then compared with that of models incorporating only two nodes, corresponding to the comparisons presented in sections 1 and 2 of the results. Next, the impact of reducing the proportion of variability explained by the mFPCA scores from 95% to 90% is investigated, incorporating the models presented in section 3. Finally, the performance of a ridge regression model is evaluated and compared with the elastic net models, section 4 of the results. 

### Comparison of Elastic Net Four Node Models 

The elastic net models with four nodes (see section 1) are all models based on the same nodes and the same predictors, with differing optimal tuning parameters with regard to the regularisation. 

The all-conditions model performed best, suggesting that information from all three conditions contributes to classification. 

The condition 1 model would be expected to perform well, given the result from the permutation test, indicating that condition 1 shows the strongest case-control differences in this condition. It performed moderately with an accuracy of 59.96% and an AUC of 0.69. However, it is clearly outperformed by the all conditions model, suggesting there is additional predictive information in conditions 2 and 3.

Overall, the all-conditions model was the strongest performer and is clearly the preferred of the two models.

### Comparison of Elastic Net Models - 4 nodes vs 2 nodes

**All Conditions Model**

The all-conditions models from sections 1 and 2 differed only in the number of EEG nodes included, with the first model using four nodes and the second using two. Subsequent differences are primarily due to the differing levels of regularisation between the two models.

Both models performed well, being the best-performing among the elastic net models, in terms of accuracy and AUC, indicating that they performed well at ranking a randomly selected case over a randomly selected control. Reducing the number of nodes has slightly increased the accuracy of the model and slightly decreased the AUC. 

As mentioned previously, the additional nodes (af7 and f7) included in the four-node analysis are supporting nodes and not the primary nodes for analysis, so while we expect that the four-node model might perform better than the two-node model, it is good to note that the models both performed well on AUC and accuracy, which is supported by our understanding the two-node model includes only the two primary nodes for analysis.

Calibration in both was quite similar; the calibration intercept is greater than 0, indicating that the observed event rate exceeds the average predicted probability; therefore, the models are systematically under-predicting the risk of schizophrenia. The calibration slope is less than 1, which is evidence of over-fitting in both models. We can see this by the limited number of predicted probabilities shown on both the rug plot and in the predicted probabilities plot.

Overall, these two models both perform well and have very similar calibration. However, the two-node model would be preferred in this case since it has a higher accuracy and a slightly better calibration, as seen in the calibration slope of 0.92 being closer to 0 than the four-node model’s calibration slope of 1.36. The Brier score as an overall model evaluation metric also suggests that the two-node model has better overall performance than the four-node model since the Brier score of 0.1236 in the two-node model is lower than 0.1544 in the four-node model.

**Condition 1 models**
The four-node condition 1 model had a lower accuracy of 59.96% and a higher AUC of 0.69 than the two-node model with an accuracy of 66.05% and an AUC of 0.629. Both models perform much worse than the all-conditions models, suggesting that conditions 2 and 3 add useful information for schizophrenia prediction.

Neither model was well calibrated, with the calibration slopes showing that both overfit to the data. The intercept suggests, however, that the model does not systematically over- or under-predict the risk of schizophrenia.

Overall, between these two condition 1 models, the four-node model is preferred due to the superior discrimination and its lower Brier score of 0.28 compared to 0.346 in the two-node model.

### Comparison of Elastic Net Models - 95% variability vs 90% variability explained

Reducing the proportion of variability explained from 95% to 90% changed both the number and composition of the retained mFPC scores. Fewer components are included under the 90% threshold, resulting in a smaller set of predictors.

The all-conditions models previously performed very well; however, here it performs far worse than before. Similarly, the condition 1 model with the 90% variability explained performs worse still than the two-node model and the four-node model. 

The all-conditions model had an AUC of 0.655 and an accuracy of 49.63%, performing worse than random guessing at our 0.5 threshold. Its Brier score is similarly quite large at 0.483. The condition 1 model performs even worse than this, with an AUC of 0.512, indicating that the model performs hardly any better than random guessing, an accuracy of 41.33%, and a Brier score of 0.576. These models are also poorly calibrated, indicating overfitting and evidence that the model systematically underpredicts the risk of schizophrenia.

The reason these models perform so much worse than previous 95% models is likely due to the mFPC scores only explaining 90% of the variability compared to 95%, which was used in all the other models. So, it was better to start out with the much larger dataset, as what was saved in terms of fewer predictors was lost in terms of predictive power. 



### Comparison of Elastic Net and Ridge Regression models

It was of interest to compare the performance of the elastic net models, in which $\alpha$ was selected using cross-validation, with ridge regression models. Both sections 1 and 4 of the results incorporated data from the same four EEG nodes and included mFPCA scores explaining 95% of the variability. Consequently, differences in model performance can be attributed primarily to the differing regularisation strategies rather than differences in the predictor set.

**All Conditions Model**

The all-conditions elastic net model used 10-fold cross-validation to identify the optimal tuning parameters of $\alpha = 0.71$ and $\lambda = 0.000081$. As the optimal value of $\alpha$ was closer to lasso ($\alpha = 1$) than ridge ($\alpha = 0$), the model placed greater emphasis on variable selection than on addressing multicollinearity. This likely reflects the high-dimensional nature of the dataset relative to the number of observations. Of the 32 mFPCA score predicted retained in the model, 0% were level 2 scores. This suggests that level 1 mFPCA scores contributed more strongly to model predictions than level 2 scores. A similar pattern was observed in the ridge regression model. Although ridge retained all 260 predictors, none of the level 2 scores were among the top 20% of coefficients ranked by absolute magnitude. Together, these findings suggest that between-subject variation contains more useful information for distinguishing schizophrenia cases from controls than trial-to-trial variation within subjects.

The superior discriminatory performance of the elastic net model, coupled with its poorer calibration, may be attributable to its variable selection properties. By removing less informative predictors and retaining those most strongly associated with case-control status, the elastic net model achieved improved discrimination. However, the model also exhibited evidence of overfitting and systematic underprediction of the probability of schizophrenia. The model favoured sparsity through coefficient selection, retaining a relatively small subset of predictors. Consequently, the estimated coefficients were comparatively large, resulting in more extreme predicted probabilities and reduced calibration performance.

In contrast, ridge regression retained all predictors, potentially reducing discrimination through the inclusion of noisy or weakly informative variables. However, the AUC was still very good (0.803), and the stronger coefficient shrinkage applied by ridge regression produced a better-calibrated model, with the 95% confidence interval for the calibration slope containing the ideal value of 1, and the 95% confidence interval for the calibration intercept closer to the ideal value of 0 than that observed for the elastic net model. This indicates improved agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. This may be because ridge regression distributes information across all predictors, producing less extreme and more evenly distributed predicted probabilities. As a result, ridge regression sacrificed some discriminatory ability in favour of improved calibration.

Overall, the elastic net and ridge regression models demonstrated different strengths in the all-conditions analysis. The elastic net model achieved stronger discrimination, while ridge regression produced better-calibrated predicted probabilities. This suggests a trade-off between variable selection and probability calibration, with elastic net better able to identify discriminatory signal and ridge regression producing more stable probability estimates.

**Condition 1 models**

The results of the individually analysed condition 1 models showed that ridge regression outperformed the elastic net model across all performance metrics, including discrimination, calibration, and classification accuracy. Although the elastic net model achieved acceptable discrimination (~0.70) and reasonable agreement between observed and predicted probabilities, it demonstrated lower accuracy and evidence of severe overfitting. In comparison the ridge regression condition 1 model showed no evidence of miscalibration, strong discrimination (AUC ~0.80) and approximately ~20% higher accuracy. 

The substantial difference in performance implies that predictors removed by the elastic net model contained useful predictive information. The superior performance of ridge regression suggests that predictive information was distributed across many mFPCA score predictors including level 2 scores that were more heavily shrunk or excluded by the elastic net model, rather than being concentrated within a small subset of components. Cross validation identified the optimal value of $\alpha = 0.81$, indicating behaviour very similar to lasso regression and a strong preference for variable selection. This pattern is consistent with a relatively dense predictive signal, whereby many predictors contribute small amounts of information. In such settings, ridge regression can outperform elastic net by preserving weak but informative signals. Furthermore, mFPCA score predictors are likely to exhibit substantial correlation, a setting in which ridge regression is often advantageous due to its ability to handle multicollinearity through coefficient shrinkage, [@ZouHastie2005; @HoerlKennard1970].

Although the elastic net model yielded a more parsimonious model by retaining only a subset of predictors, the primary objective of this study was predictive performance. Consequently, the ridge regression model was preferred for condition 1.

Interestingly, the condition 1 ridge regression model also outperformed the corresponding ridge regression model fitted using data from all conditions. While the discriminatory ability of the two models was similar, the condition 1 model demonstrated improved calibration, particularly with respect to the calibration intercept and the agreement between predicted and observed probabilities. This finding is consistent with the permutation t-test results, which suggested that condition 1 contained the strongest differences between schizophrenia cases and controls and was therefore likely to be the most informative condition for prediction.

**Condition 2 and 3 models**

Since ridge regression yielded the strongest performance for condition 1, the same modelling approach was subsequently applied to conditions 2 and 3. Although neither condition performed as well as condition 1, both achieved better predictive performance than expected, demonstrating good discrimination and classification accuracy. However, the calibration metrics for condition 2 suggested that the model was overfitted and systematically underpredicted the probability of schizophrenia. The condition 3 model performed somewhat better, with the 95% confidence interval for the calibration slope containing the ideal value of 1. Nevertheless, the calibration intercept indicated that the model still systematically underpredicted risk.

The relatively good predictive performance of conditions 2 and 3 was somewhat surprising given the permutation t-test results, which identified condition 1 as the sensory condition exhibiting the strongest differences between schizophrenia cases and controls. However, these findings are consistent with previous research demonstrating that neural activity differs between schizophrenia cases and controls even in the absence of external sensory stimulation. Recent systematic reviews of resting-state EEG and MEG (magnetoencephalography) studies have reported widespread electrophysiological abnormalities in schizophrenia, indicating altered spontaneous neural activity and functional connectivity during resting-state conditions [@DePieri2025; @Liu2025].

Although the ridge regression models for conditions 2 and 3 performed better than expected, neither outperformed the corresponding condition 1 model. This suggests that while all three sensory conditions contained predictive information, condition 1 remained the most informative condition for distinguishing schizophrenia cases from controls.


### Overall

<!-- Overall, the best-performing models were the all-conditions elastic net models using mFPCA scores that explained 95% of the variability in the data.  -->

<!-- The condition 1 elastic net model using 4 nodes did not perform badly either, and it performed better than condition 2 or 3, which is as we would expect from the results of the permutation test.  -->

<!-- However, the superior performance of the all-conditions models from each of the four results sections suggests that there is likely some important information contained in the condition 2 and condition 3 scores, as the model with all conditions performed the best of the elastic net and ridge regression models. -->

The best-performing model overall was the condition 1 ridge regression model, which achieved an AUC of 0.795. The 95% confidence interval for the calibration slope contained the ideal value of 1, while the 95% confidence interval for the calibration intercept contained the ideal value of 0, indicating good agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. The model also achieved a classification accuracy of 79.88% and a low Brier score of 0.1555. Collectively, these performance metrics indicate a well-performing classification model with good discrimination, calibration, and overall predictive accuracy.

### Strengths and Limitations

A key strength of this study was the use of Functional Data Analysis techniques to analyse EEG signals as continuous functions, in particular, the application of mFPCA which allowed the incorporation of the repeated-trial structure of the data. Another strength was the successful development of a predictive model for schizophrenia using these mFPCA-derived scores. Elastic Net regression proved a suitable choice due to the large amount of correlated predictor variables, simultaneously balancing variable shrinkage and selection. Furthermore, several analyses produced consistent findings, with Condition 1 emerging as the most informative condition across both the permutation tests and Elastic Net models. This consistency furthers confidence in the robustness of overall findings.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. Firstly, following the overall train-test split of the data set, the number of unique subjects for model development was relatively small which limits the statistical power of analysis. Secondly, potential over-fitting is observed within the Elastic Net models due to the large number of predictors retained within a model compared with the number of subjects. Finally, the analysis focused on a few pre-determined EEG nodes which are commonly associated with schizophrenia rather than the entire electrode set. This means potential informative signals from other brain regions were not investigated which may produce meaningful results.

Despite these limitations, the study demonstrated that mFPCA combined with elastic net classification was an accurate framework for investigating the EEG abnormalities associated with schizophrenia.

##Comparison with other studies

In modern EEG analysis, FDA is a common tool, as it allows curves to be analysed as a whole, enabling interpretability and the development of accurate prediction models [@yi2022classification, @zhang2020prediction]. 

However, when it comes to classification models for schizophrenia based on EEG signals, few use a functional data approach instead, opting for more novel machine learning approaches, such as in @SABETI2011, in which they performed a new feature selection method and used both linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and adaptive boosting (Adaboost) to classify subjects as cases or controls. These models had an accuracy of 85.9% and 91.4%, respectively and found that their feature selection method outperformed a PCA-based feature selection. 

Another approach used a neural network classification model to diagnose schizophrenia. The model has a balanced accuracy and precision of 93% and shows improved accuracy compared to other traditional algorithms such as random forest and K-nearest neighbour [@lujan2023accurate].

A review of deep learning models for schizophrenia diagnosis, @ranjan2024deep, found that convolutional neural networks were the most commonly employed model for mental health diagnosis. By comparing many different models, it was found that the 2D-CNN model had the highest classification performance, with an accuracy of 99.5%, while the other models included in the review also had accuracies over 90%.

Using FDA, our analysis is much simpler than that of a neural network, which, although it has great prediction accuracy, lacks interpretability. Also, these neural networks require large datasets with many subjects, which would not have been appropriate for our dataset, which had only 40 subjects. As suggested in @SABETI2011, a more specialised feature selection process may have improved the accuracy of our models. Similarly, it is highly possible that our data were nonlinear and comparing our model with another approach, such as boosting or random forest, may have given a higher accuracy in our mFPCA-based elastic net model.

## Further Research

Future work could include a larger number of participants within the study to improve the accuracy and reliability of results. With the addition of a number of trials and nodes, a complete picture could be created of the subject-level and trial-level variation within the study.

It could also be interesting to apply FPCA to multiple conditions and trials to investigate the consistency of Condition 1 results throughout the data set. Finally, while the Elastic Net model achieved strong discriminatory performance, future studies could explore alternative classification techniques, such as random forests or neural networks. Comparing multiple findings in this way could provide further insight into the predictive value of mFPCA scores.

# Conclusion

In conclusion, we found that there was a significant difference in the EEG curves of individuals with schizophrenia and controls in condition 1, since the permutation t-test showed pointwise significance in many parts and global significance in others. The effect was less in condition 2 however there was a small pointwise significant difference post-stimulus, and in condition 3 there is no pointwise significance. This supports the hypothesis that sensory gating deficits are most evident when participants generate an expected auditory stimulus through their own action, condition 1 in this study.

Using functional data analysis we analysed and decomposed EEG curves into functional principal components to develop a classification model that can discriminate well between individuals with schizophrenia and controls. Our best models were the all conditions model using 2 and 4 nodes respectively where mFPC scores were found from the eigenfunctions that explained 95% of the variability in the curves. These were followed by the four-node model of condition 1 where mFPCs explained 95% of the variability in the curves, in terms of model performance. This is likely due to the sensory gating process discussed previously. The condition 2 and condition 3 models did not perform well however, the inclusion of condition 2 and 3 alongside condition 1 appears to provide additional information that improves the predictive power of the model.

Further work could be done with a larger set of subjects in order to improve the generalisability of this model as the calibration was poor and all models in the validation set.
